title: Cross-host 64-byte line dedup inside a shared CXL pool
idea: Box: dedup × CXL pool controller × 64 B line × on write × SRAM hash index. The pool controller hashes each incoming line, keeps one physical copy with a refcount, and redirects duplicates through a two-level remap table, so dozens of hosts running the same OS, libraries and model weights share lines across machine boundaries.
why: Capacity: co-located VMs and inference replicas carry 20–50% duplicate content; pooled line dedup claims 1.3–2× effective pool capacity, i.e. 25–50% lower cost per usable bit with no new cell technology.

title: HBM base die Huffman-codes BF16 exponent planes on write
idea: Box: lossless entropy coding × HBM logic base die × 4 KB tensor tile × on write × static Huffman on the exponent plane. The base die splits BF16 words into raw sign/mantissa planes and an exponent plane coded at ~2.6 bits instead of 8, re-expanding on read, so the stack transparently holds and moves fewer bits.
why: Weights and KV dominate HBM and their exponents carry little entropy; ~1.4× capacity and TSV bandwidth per stack, softening the HBM wafer-area tax (fact 6) and data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: Park idle chat sessions as token IDs, re-prefill in FLOP valleys
idea: Box: recompute × inference runtime × whole-session KV × idle >30 s × backing = 2-byte token IDs. Idle sessions drop their KV cache (~100–300 KB per token for large models) and keep only token IDs; when the user returns, a scheduler re-prefills the context in bursts on compute left idle between decode steps.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bytes at ~10^5:1 compression of parked state; cuts resident KV in multi-tenant chat serving 3–10× because most sessions are idle most of the time.

title: KV cache whose precision decays with token age and attention
idea: Box: approximate × KV manager × 16-token block × age-triggered × format ladder FP16→FP8→INT4→INT2→evict. A background re-quantizer demotes blocks as they age and as their accumulated attention mass stays low, while sink tokens and recently attended blocks stay at full precision.
why: Attention mass concentrates on recent and a few anchor tokens; an average of 3–4 bits per value instead of 16 shrinks long-context KV 4–5×.

title: Line-granular copy-on-write for forks, snapshots and VM clones
idea: Box: share × MMU plus memory controller × 64 B line (not 4 KB page) × first write × per-page 64-bit diverged-line mask. Cloned pages keep pointing at the parent frame; a write copies only the touched line into a small overlay frame, and the controller merges parent and overlay on reads using the mask.
why: Serverless snapshots, VM clones and forked workers duplicate a full 4 KB page to change a few bytes; line CoW cuts post-fork memory growth 5–20×, packing more instances per GB.

title: Sub-page hardware meshing merges fragmented heap pages without moving objects
idea: Box: defragment × page-table extension × 1 KB chunk × background scan × chunk-mask PTE. A 4-bit chunk map in each PTE lets two virtual pages whose live 1 KB chunks do not overlap share one physical frame, so the allocator reclaims fragmentation while every pointer stays valid.
why: Fragmentation wastes 15–40% of RSS in long-running C/C++ services; hardware meshing recovers most of it, ~1.2–1.5× effective density.

title: Derivable pages: kernel drops memory it can recompute from recipes
idea: Box: recompute × OS kernel × page × memory pressure × registered recipe handle. Applications mark pages as derived (decompressed libraries, parsed configs, dequantized weights, JIT code) with a callback; under pressure the kernel discards them like clean page cache and re-runs the recipe on fault instead of swapping.
why: A large share of anonymous memory is a cache of cheap computation; making it reclaimable cuts provisioned DRAM 10–30% with no swap I/O.

title: Near-duplicate KV blocks share a base plus 4-bit residual
idea: Box: approximate dedup × GPU KV pool × 16-token block × LSH on key vectors × shared base + sparse quantized residual. Blocks from different requests (edited system prompts, popular RAG documents, boilerplate code) whose keys fall within a tolerance are stored once with tiny per-request residuals.
why: Exact prefix sharing misses near-duplicates; merging them adds 1.5–3× effective KV capacity in RAG and agent serving.

title: Seed-generated weights: LFSR seeds plus coefficients replace stored matrices
idea: Box: procedural generation × accelerator load path × 8×8 weight block × decode at GEMM time × 16-bit LFSR seed + 4 coefficients. Each block is a fitted combination of pseudo-random basis vectors regenerated by an on-chip LFSR, so memory holds ~3–4 bits per weight with no codebook to fetch.
why: 4–5× less weight memory than BF16 and fewer bytes moved per FLOP; logic is cheap while DRAM bits are scarce.

title: Controller dictionary stores the 4,096 commonest lines as 12-bit handles
idea: Box: dictionary dedup × memory controller × 64 B line × on write × epoch-learned value table. The controller keeps a hardware dictionary of frequent full-line values (zeros, fill patterns, padding, one-hot rows) and stores matching lines as 12-bit handles in compact pages, refreshing the dictionary at epoch boundaries.
why: Zero and pattern lines are 10–30% of memory in many workloads; holding them at 12 bits per line gives 1.15–1.4× capacity for a few mm² of logic.

title: Reed–Solomon striping replaces triple replication in in-memory stores
idea: Box: redundancy reduction × distributed key-value tier × object stripe × on write × RS(6,3) with NIC offload. Objects are striped across nodes with parity encoded by the NIC; reads gather data fragments in parallel over RDMA, with decode only on failure.
why: Durability overhead drops from 3× to 1.5×, halving DRAM for replicated caches and session stores fleetwide.

title: Scheduler anti-phases jobs' memory peaks, provisioning for p95 not peak
idea: Box: time-multiplex × cluster scheduler × job × forecast-triggered × small CXL burst pool. Each job's footprint curve is forecast (shuffle phases, eval passes, nightly batches) and jobs are packed so peaks interleave; rare collisions borrow from a small rack burst pool.
why: Servers are sized for peak and peak-to-mean ratios run 1.5–3×; anti-phase packing can cut installed DRAM 20–35%.

title: Bit-plane weight layout: one stored copy serves every precision tier
idea: Box: progressive precision × memory layout × bit-plane × per-request policy × MSB-first planes. Weights are stored as bit-planes so a request tier or insensitive layer fetches only the top k planes, replacing separate 8-, 4- and 3-bit copies of the same model.
why: Serving fleets keep 2–4 quantized copies per model; one progressive copy saves ~2–3× across a model zoo and cuts bytes read for low tiers.

title: Fixed-rate ZFP codec in the L2 fill path for simulation arrays
idea: Box: lossy random-access compression × L2 fill/evict path × 4×4×4 float block × fixed 8–16 bits per value × HPC fields. Arrays live in DRAM as fixed-rate ZFP blocks; a cache-side codec decompresses on fill and recompresses on eviction, so code sees plain doubles.
why: HPC mesh size per node is DRAM-bound; 4–8× capacity at error below discretization error.

title: Learned models plus Elias–Fano offsets replace pointer-heavy indexes
idea: Box: representation shrink × database engine × index × build time × piecewise-linear model + succinct leaf offsets. B-tree inner nodes and hash-index pointers become small learned position models with Elias–Fano coded offsets queried by rank/select.
why: Indexes take 20–50% of in-memory database DRAM; learned plus succinct encodings shrink them 10–100×.

title: Garbage collector compresses cold object subgraphs behind forwarding stubs
idea: Box: compression × managed-runtime GC × object subgraph × untouched for N cycles × read-barrier inflate. During marking the runtime serializes cold subgraphs into compressed blobs and installs stubs; a read barrier inflates them on first touch.
why: Managed heaps run 2–5× larger than live data and much of it is cold; cold-object compression cuts heap 30–50%.

title: Shadow router prefetches next-layer MoE experts from CXL flash
idea: Box: tiering × MoE inference runtime × expert × predicted one layer early × CXL-attached low-latency NAND. A tiny predictor maps the current hidden state to the next layer's likely experts, which stream into a small HBM expert cache while the current layer computes.
why: MoE models leave >90% of parameters idle per token; holding only active plus predicted experts shrinks resident weights 4–8×.

title: Internal exchange leases stranded server DRAM by the GB-minute
idea: Box: share × datacenter market × GB-minute × auction-triggered × CXL switch or RDMA delivery. Each server offers its idle DRAM on an internal exchange; jobs bid for GB-minutes delivered over the pooled fabric and owners' budgets are credited.
why: 25–40% of fleet DRAM sits idle at any moment; recapturing it cuts new DRAM purchases 10–25%.

title: Tensor-train embedding cores with a full-precision hot-ID cache
idea: Box: factorization × recommendation model × embedding row × lookup-time reconstruction × TT cores + hot-row cache. Huge embedding tables become tensor-train cores reconstructed per lookup, with the hottest ~1% of IDs cached at full precision.
why: Embedding tables are the biggest DRAM consumer in recommender fleets; TT plus hot cache shrinks them 10–100× at small accuracy cost.

title: Gist tokens replace old context; raw chunks re-expand from flash
idea: Box: summarize × agent runtime × document chunk × leaves recent window × raw tokens on SSD. Older chunks are replaced by a few learned gist tokens' KV; if attention to a gist crosses a threshold the runtime re-prefills the original chunk from flash (zoom-in).
why: Million-token agents carry enormous KV; gist plus zoom keeps it ~20× smaller with recoverable fidelity.

title: Per-feature byte budgets enforced in CI at contract DRAM price
idea: Box: governance × software process × service feature × every merge × bytes-per-request metric. Each service declares resident-set and bytes-per-request budgets; CI profiles memory, blocks merges over budget, and dashboards price each MB at the current DRAM contract price.
why: Software memory bloat grows ~10–20% a year; priced budgets bend demand 10–30% when DRAM costs 4× more.

title: Single coherent copy shared by CPU, GPU and NIC kills bounce buffers
idea: Box: eliminate copies × coherent fabric × buffer × allocation time × one physical copy over CXL.cache or chip-to-chip links. Pipelines that hold the same tensor in pinned host memory, GPU memory and NIC staging use one coherent allocation with zero-copy DMA.
why: Staging and bounce buffers occupy 10–30% of host DRAM in AI servers; removing two of three copies frees most of it.

title: Profile-guided compiler narrows over-wide fields with overflow traps
idea: Box: representation shrink × compiler × struct field × profile-guided × narrow + reorder + trap. Fields whose observed ranges fit fewer bits (int64 counters under 2^20, enums, flags) are narrowed and packed, with cheap overflow traps that re-widen via deoptimization.
why: Padding and over-wide fields waste 20–40% of in-memory object bytes.

title: Reflash SSDs to zoned mode, lend freed FTL DRAM via CMB
idea: Box: repurpose × installed NVMe SSDs × controller DRAM (~1 GB per TB) × firmware reflash × NVMe Controller Memory Buffer. Switching drives to zoned/host-managed mapping frees the controller DRAM that held the FTL table, which firmware then exposes to the host as a PCIe-mapped CMB for I/O buffers, queues and spill of warm data.
why: Every installed 30 TB SSD carries ~30 GB of DRAM; reclaiming it adds host-usable memory with zero new wafers, so no new fluorinated etch gases, PFAS resists or fluoropolymer parts are consumed.

title: Idle inference GPUs lend free HBM as host swap
idea: Box: harvest × installed GPU fleet × 2 MB page × idle windows × PCIe/NVLink peer access. A kernel driver exposes unused HBM on idle or lightly loaded GPUs as a fast swap device for CPU hosts and reclaims it within milliseconds when a large kernel needs it.
why: Off-peak, 30–60% of fleet HBM sits empty; borrowing already-fabricated memory replaces new DIMMs and needs no new fluorinated fab chemistry.

title: Run cache-sized services on gigabyte-LLC CPUs with minimal DIMMs
idea: Box: substitute × existing large-L3 CPUs (~1 GB stacked SRAM) × whole working set × deployment time × minimal DIMM population. Routers, rate limiters, feature-flag and session services whose working sets fit in ~1 GB are pinned to large-cache parts already in the fleet, with one small DIMM per channel.
why: Those services get 256–512 GB per box by default; running them cache-resident frees 80–95% of their DRAM using installed silicon, so nothing new passes through fluorinated etch or PFAS lithography.

title: Pool memory over polyolefin twinax and acrylate-coated fiber, no FEP
idea: Box: pool × rack interconnect × rack × deployment × foamed PE/PP-insulated twinax + Ge-core silica fiber with urethane-acrylate coating. CXL memory-pooling fabrics are cabled with fluorine-free dielectrics and connectors, and retimers equalize the slightly higher loss so a PFAS ban does not block pooling.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM 10–25% fleetwide, but default high-speed cables use FEP/PTFE; a fluorine-free cable bill of materials keeps that saving deployable.

title: Retired FPGA SmartNICs host retired DDR4 as memory expanders
idea: Box: reuse × decommissioned FPGA boards × DIMM × redeployment × PCIe-attached memory-controller bitstream. Retired FPGA cards are reprogrammed as memory controllers for tested DDR4 RDIMMs harvested from retired servers and exposed as a warm tier for page cache and KV spill.
why: Both parts already exist: zero new wafer starts and so zero new fluorinated chemistry, while a near-free warm tier absorbs 20–30% of a host's capacity demand.

title: Frozen shared interpreter heaps mapped by every worker process
idea: Box: share × language runtime × immutable object arena × interpreter startup × mmap-shared snapshot. Python/Node/Ruby servers freeze imported modules, bytecode, constants and read-only model data into a snapshot arena mapped read-only by all workers, with immortal objects so refcount writes no longer un-share pages.
why: Multi-worker servers duplicate hundreds of MB per worker; sharing frozen arenas cuts their RSS 30–60% with a pure software change and no fluorinated inputs.

title: Fluorine-free mature-node fab builds page-compression co-processors
idea: Box: new hardware × 180 nm-class CMOS × 4 KB page compressor × fab route × i-line DNQ/novolac resist, photo-definable BCB dielectric, Cl2/HBr/BCl3 etch, O2/Cl2 chamber clean, H2-bake oxide removal, hot-phosphoric nitride strip. Vias are defined lithographically in photo-BCB rather than etched in oxide, so no CF4/C4F8/NF3/SF6, HF or PFAS photoacid is used, and the chips act as PCIe zswap accelerators.
why: Shows memory-saving silicon can be built under a full PFAS ban on a low-capital line; arrays of these compress cold pages ~2.5–3×, freeing 15–25% of host DRAM.

title: Ternary weights packed five trits per byte with LUT decode
idea: Box: representation shrink × model training × weights × train time × 3^5 = 243 states in 8 bits + table decode. Models trained natively ternary store five weights per byte and decode via a 256-entry table held in registers or shared memory.
why: 1.6 bits per weight versus 16 is a 10× weight-memory cut, achieved with algorithms and existing GPUs only, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Discounted soft-RAM VMs back 30% of memory with compressed tiers
idea: Box: oversubscribe × cloud pricing × VM × customer opt-in × compressed and remote backing. A VM class sells nominal memory at a discount where the coldest 30% is backed by compressed or remote memory under a published p99 fault-latency SLO.
why: Lets providers overcommit ~1.3× on installed hardware; pricing plus software only, so no new fluorinated fab inputs.

title: Memory-efficient device certification with per-GB-avoided credits
idea: Box: demand reallocation × consumer OS and procurement × device SKU × certification × zram + app freeze-to-flash + shared web engine. Phones and laptops that pass a responsiveness benchmark with less DRAM earn a label and a per-GB-avoided credit funded by datacenter buyers.
why: Consumer devices take roughly half of DRAM bits; a 25% trim there frees ~10% of world supply for servers without building anything, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Idle containers hibernate to NVMe and restore pages lazily
idea: Box: evict whole process × orchestrator × container × idle >N s × checkpoint image + userfaultfd lazy page-in. Idle services are checkpointed to local flash and their memory freed; a request wakes them in milliseconds with pages faulted in on demand.
why: 30–50% of containers are idle at any moment; reclaiming their RSS cuts node DRAM 15–30% with software only and no fluorinated inputs.

title: Speculative decoding lets big models live in host DRAM, not HBM
idea: Box: amortize × decode algorithm × k-token draft window × per step × target weights in installed host DDR. A small draft model in HBM proposes k tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass, so each large-model weight read is amortized over k×batch tokens and its weights can sit in slower, already-installed host memory.
why: Cuts HBM needed per served model 3–5× by tolerating lower weight bandwidth; algorithm-only on existing servers, so no new fluorinated chemistry.

title: Reversible layers reconstruct activations instead of storing them
idea: Box: invertibility × model architecture × layer activations × backward pass × additive coupling blocks. Training uses invertible residual blocks whose inputs are recomputed exactly from outputs during backpropagation, so per-layer activations are never kept.
why: Activation memory becomes constant in depth, 5–10× less training memory; mathematics only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Allocation-time hash-consing of immutable values in managed runtimes
idea: Box: dedup × runtime allocator × immutable object × at allocation × concurrent table of canonical instances. Strings, tuples, boxed numbers, decoded JSON subtrees and records marked immutable are looked up on allocation and replaced by a canonical shared instance.
why: Data-heavy services carry 20–40% duplicate immutable objects; canonicalization reclaims most of it in software, with no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Page-aligned content-defined packaging so kernel dedup actually hits
idea: Box: dedup enablement × build and packaging toolchain × 4 KB/2 MB chunk × build time × content-defined chunking with alignment padding. Binaries, container layers and model files are laid out so identical content lands on identical page boundaries across versions and tenants, letting existing same-page merging match it.
why: Small offsets defeat page dedup today; alignment lifts merge rates from a few percent to 20–40% on dense hosts, a pure toolchain change free of fluorinated chemistry.

title: Count-min and HyperLogLog sketches replace exact per-key stream state
idea: Box: probabilistic sketch × stream processor × per-key state × continuous × bounded-error counters. Counting, distinct and top-k operators keep fixed-size sketches with ~1% error bounds instead of exact per-key hash maps.
why: Per-key state stores reach terabytes; sketches cut them 100–1000× where approximate answers suffice; software only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: GPU texture units decode block-compressed weights at zero ALU cost
idea: Box: decompress × existing GPU texture-sampling hardware × 4×4 block × every fetch × BC4/BC5 (ASTC on mobile) endpoint-plus-index format. Weights are encoded as single- or dual-channel block-compressed textures by an encoder that minimizes matmul output error, and kernels fetch them through the texture path, which decompresses in fixed-function hardware.
why: ~4 bits per weight (4× smaller than FP16) with free random-access decode on silicon already shipped in every GPU, so no new chips and no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Hardware video encoders compress parked KV caches as 10-bit frames
idea: Box: lossy compression × existing GPU video engines × per-head KV tensor × session parked × HEVC 10-bit with channel-reordered frames. Parked KV caches are reordered so tokens become frame time and channels become pixels, then encoded by idle on-die video engines and decoded on resume.
why: If token-to-token correlation holds, parked KV shrinks 5–10× using fixed-function engines already shipped; no new silicon, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Turn off memory mirroring and rank sparing; checkpoint in software
idea: Box: remove redundancy × BIOS RAS settings × channel/rank × fleet policy × application checkpoint and replication. Servers configured for mirroring (50% of capacity lost) or rank sparing (12–25%) are switched to full capacity, with reliability provided by software checkpoints and service-level replication.
why: Reclaims stranded capacity on installed hardware immediately; configuration only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Retrain tokenizers for fewer tokens per document, shrinking KV
idea: Box: fewer tokens × tokenizer × token × next model refresh × larger multilingual/code-aware vocabulary with frequent multi-word merges. New model generations adopt tokenizers that encode the same text in 20–30% fewer tokens, and KV size scales with token count.
why: 20–30% less KV per context at long context, outweighing the larger embedding table; software only, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Price LLM APIs per KV-gigabyte-second to shape context demand
idea: Box: demand shaping × API pricing × request × billing × KV-GB-second meter with shared-prefix discounts. Customers pay for the memory-time their context occupies, with discounts for shared prefixes and short sessions, nudging agents to summarize and reuse.
why: Makes the scarce resource visible to buyers; a 20–30% drop in average resident context is plausible using only billing logic, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Repurpose installed Optane PMem as read-only weight and index tier
idea: Box: reuse × installed persistent-memory DIMMs × 256 B block × deployment × DAX-mapped read-mostly data. Fleets still holding discontinued 3D XPoint DIMMs map read-mostly data (model weights, inverted indexes, embedding tables) straight into the address space, sparing DRAM for write-heavy state.
why: Byte-addressable ~300 ns capacity already sitting in racks absorbs read-mostly working sets; no new production, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Online miss-ratio curves right-size every in-memory cache
idea: Box: right-size × every application cache × cache instance × continuous × spatially sampled miss-ratio curve. Each cache samples ~0.1% of keys to build its miss-ratio curve online, and an operator shrinks caches to the knee where the marginal MB stops buying hits.
why: Caches are sized by guesswork; MRC-driven sizing typically frees 20–50% of cache memory at equal hit rate, software only, no fluorinated inputs.
